summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Identity-document rules are the fastest-moving area of restriction at state level. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, with rights groups describing the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the documents a visitor is asked to produce are read against the rules of the state they are standing in.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is not theoretical: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Within that national picture, Tennessee's Adult Entertainment Act (2023, SB 3/HB 9) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment', a definition that explicitly includes 'male or female impersonators', on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony carrying 1 to 6 years and fines to $3,000. The reach of the definition means gender-expression itself, not the content of a performance, is what the statute penalises, so public visibility carries criminal exposure rather than only venue-level licensing consequences.

The statute is enforceable and current. It survived federal challenge on procedural grounds, the appeals-court ruling upholding it stands after the Supreme Court refused to hear the challenges in February 2025, and a separate suit brought by performers remains ongoing.

A further Tennessee measure narrows access to shelter. Under the 2026 'Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act', trans women are barred from women's shelters, which removes a common emergency resource for a trans visitor in distress.
tangentialFactors:
Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Assessments of internal risk are similarly stark. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

Violence data place Tennessee in the worst-performing group. A national analysis of July 2026 using TGEU and Williams Institute figures puts Tennessee's killing rate of trans women at 7.8 per 100,000 per year, derived from 10 recorded deaths between 2008 and 2025 and treated as an undercount floor, and grades the state in the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier.

The Adult Entertainment Act is unusual in kind as well as severity: it converts a public presence that reads as gender-nonconforming into a misdemeanour or felony, where most state-level restrictions operate through facility rules or document policy. That difference shapes what a trans visitor should expect in Tennessee rather than in a state whose restrictions stop at bathrooms or licences.
localsOnly:
The Tennessee State Legislature passed a bill in April 2024 banning gender-affirming care for Tennessee inmates, removing access to transition-related treatment for residents in state custody.

The 2026 'Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act' requires transgender inmates to be placed in prisons according to sex assigned at birth, and separately bans trans women from women's shelters. Residents therefore face both custody-placement rules and a loss of shelter access on top of the document rules that apply nationwide.

The Adult Entertainment Act's penalties fall most heavily on local performers and venues: a Class A misdemeanour with up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine on a first offence, and a Class E felony of 1 to 6 years with fines to $3,000 on a second, for 'adult cabaret entertainment' defined to include 'male or female impersonators' on public property or where a child could see it.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records an enforcement action under the Adult Entertainment Act against a visitor, or a count of charges brought since enactment. Whether the statute has been used against gender-expression rather than staged performance in practice is unresolved.

The separate challenge to the Adult Entertainment Act brought by performers is described as ongoing, but its subject matter, forum and likely timing are not stated in the sources.

Whether the 2026 shelter prohibition applies to privately run, federally funded or all shelters is not specified in the sources, and the same is true of the prison-placement mandate's interaction with federal custody standards.

Bathroom and facility rules specific to Tennessee are not sourced here; the counts given are national. Whether Tennessee permits gender-marker changes on licences or birth certificates is likewise not stated in this inventory and remains unverified.

The 7.8 per 100,000 killing rate rests on 10 recorded deaths over seventeen years and is expressly described as a floor, so the true figure and the comparison basis against other states are unresolved.
